claims.claim: Random 5-fold CV gave 0.995 and GroupKFold gave 0.468 on 200 simulated respondents with 5 waves each and a person-level random label.
claims.source: Run with scikit-learn 1.8.0 and 1.9.1, RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=0), in this repository.

concept_html:
Three sets, three jobs:

  • Training rows fit the model.
  • Validation rows, or cross-validation folds within training, choose between models and settings.
  • Test rows measure the final choice, once. Every extra look at the test set turns it into a second validation set, and its score stops being an honest estimate.

Split so the test set looks like the data the model will meet.

Stratify on the target when a class is rare. train_test_split(X, y, stratify=y) keeps a 3% positive rate at 3% in both sets. Without it, a small test set can end up with very few positives.

Group when rows are not independent. A panel respondent answering five waves appears in five rows. A random row split puts some of their waves in training and others in test. The model then recognises the person instead of learning the pattern, and the test score measures memory.

A demonstration from this course's build (scikit-learn 1.8, random forest): 200 simulated respondents, 5 waves each, a label that depends only on the person and is unrelated to the features. Random 5-fold CV reported accuracy 0.995. GroupKFold by respondent reported 0.468: chance, which is the truth.

The group is whatever repeats: respondent, household, store, patient, device. If it will be new in production, keep it out of training in validation too. For time-ordered use, split by time as well (lesson B10-L3).

Record the split: the seed, the group column, and the resulting row counts, in the run manifest (lesson B6-L2).

lines: import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit
def split_by_group(
df: pd.DataFrame, group_col: str, test_size: float, seed: int
) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.DataFrame]:
"""Split so that no group appears in both train and test."""
splitter = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, test_size=test_size, random_state=seed)
train_idx, test_idx = next(splitter.split(df, groups=df[group_col]))
return df.iloc[train_idx], df.iloc[test_idx]

exercises.solution:
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit


def split_by_group(
    df: pd.DataFrame, group_col: str, test_size: float, seed: int
) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.DataFrame]:
    """Split rows so no group appears in both train and test.

    Args:
        df: Rows to split.
        group_col: Column identifying the repeated unit, such as respondent.
        test_size: Share of groups in the test set.
        seed: Random seed for reproducibility.

    Returns:
        (train, test).
    """
    splitter = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, test_size=test_size, random_state=seed)
    train_idx, test_idx = next(splitter.split(df, groups=df[group_col]))
    return df.iloc[train_idx], df.iloc[test_idx]

title: Train, validation and test, split by the right unit
why_html: A model predicting survey drop-out was validated with a random row split over a panel dataset. It scored AUC 0.93. Deployed on a newly recruited panel, where every respondent was new, it scored 0.61. Each respondent's answering style had let the model match test rows to the same person's training rows. A group split would have shown 0.61 before deployment.
